t: Length of the Longest Alphabetical Continuous Substring
o: We need the longest substring of `s` that appears as a contiguous piece of "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz", i.e., a maximal run where each character is exactly one more than the previous. In "abacaba" the runs are "ab", "a", "c", "ab" — longest length 2. In "abcde" the whole string qualifies, length 5. With n up to 1e5 we want a single linear pass: extend the current run while `s[i] == s[i-1] + 1`, otherwise restart at 1.
k: A run continues exactly when s[i] is the alphabet-successor of s[i-1]; track run lengths in one pass.

a.i: Keep the length of the current continuous run ending at index i. If s[i] follows s[i-1] in the alphabet, extend it; otherwise reset to 1. The answer is the maximum seen.
s: For each i ≥ 1: cur = cur + 1 if s[i] == s[i-1] + 1 else 1.
Update best with cur; return best.

a.n: Approach 2: Check all substrings via expansion
a.i: For each starting index, expand rightward while characters keep increasing by one; record the extent. This is the same recurrence viewed as per-start expansion and is a natural brute force that still runs in O(n) total because each character is visited once across all expansions when implemented with the running-length trick.
s: For each start i, walk forward while consecutive letters increase by one.
Equivalent to the linear scan but framed per-start.
a.t: O(n) — jumps past each maximal run

w: Both are effectively the same O(n) idea; present the run-length scan as primary. Edge cases: single-character strings return 1; runs cannot exceed 26 ('z' breaks any continuation). Follow-up: return the substring itself — track the start index of the best run.
